The Sovereign Compact: Credentialed Merit, Performative Slogans, and the Strategic Realignment of American Politics 

(Volume I of II)

DIOGENES REIPUBLICAE AMERICANAE

Master Table of Contents

• Preface: The Sovereign Equation (Volume I)

• Part I: My Man Buchanan: The Blueprint of Economic Protectionism (Volume I)

• Part II: The Cyclical Paradox and the "Confederate Corner" (Volume I)

• Part III: The FBA Alignment and the Recovery of Basics (Volume I)

• Part IV: Geopolitical Totemism, Christian Zionism, and the Split Allegiance (Volume I)

• Part V: The Failure of Establishment Propaganda (Volume II)

• Part VI: The Techno-Oligarch Fallacy and the "Smartest Guy" Syndrome (Volume II)

• Part VII: The Sovereign Compact and the Primary Construct (Volume II)

Preface: The Sovereign Equation

This document establishes an uncompromised, structurally rigorous critique of the contemporary American political landscape. It rejects the focus focused scripts of the political consultant class and the emotional volatility of tribal polarization. By applying historical microeconomic models, generational data, and a strict baseline of institutional reverence, this analysis strips away the performative marketing that currently paralyzes domestic governance. True intellectual rigor demands that we evaluate political movements, foreign alliances, and structural systems dispassionately measuring every actor solely by their adherence to constitutional law, fiscal discipline, and sovereign loyalty to the American republic.

Part I: My Man Buchanan: The Blueprint of Economic Protectionism

American conservatism is structurally broken because it has decoupled itself from the material reality of resource scarcity and historical context. At its theoretical inception, conservatism operates not as a performative cultural brand, but as an institutional brake the macro level manifestation of the household balance sheet. When a domestic unit experiences an extraction of capital or a reduction in labor hours, a rational manager does not engage in speculative, unfunded external ventures. Every allocation of capital toward a new project must be strictly offset by a corresponding expenditure reduction elsewhere.

At the national scale, this stabilizing role has been abandoned for culture war theater. The modern populist movement is less an ideological conservative awakening and more a populist coalition of disaffected, historically working class voters whose parents and grandparents were traditional New Deal Democrats. Massively alienated by an elite left that traded labor for corporate interest groups and fluid identity politics, these voters grabbed onto an untraditional actor precisely because he refused to play by the rules of a broken establishment. While this systemic disruption is a logical reaction to elite capture, wrapping a movement in a flag is performative marketing it is not conservatism.

True conservatism requires an intellectual foundation grounded in generational continuity and historical fact. My economic alignment remains rooted in the Pat Buchanan tradition of economic protectionism. Mainstream, free market economists routinely panic at the mention of tariffs and immigration restrictions, arguing that artificial boundaries violate pure globalist market constructs. They completely miss the structural nuance of Buchanan’s framework. 

He recognized that the American economic boom of the 1950s and 1960s was an artificial historical anomaly born from the physical destruction of European and Asian industrial bases in World War II The United States possessed a temporary global monopoly because it was the only industrial power left standing with its infrastructure intact.
Buchanan knew this monopoly would inevitably collapse once foreign manufacturing rebuilt . He accurately predicted that an unhedged "free trade" apparatus would incentivize corporate boardrooms to prioritize short-term shareholder wealth over domestic stability. 

When companies accumulate that volume of liquid capital, the wealth inherently corrupts the system, stripping away any institutional or geographical loyalty to the working class. Today, we see elite oligarchs rubbing their hands together, looking at America as nothing but an un regulated balance sheet to exploit. These techno billionaires believe that because they have capital, they have a blank check to dismantle regulations and bypass the American Constitution. They trade the security of our nation for global corporate profits.

Because Buchanan's protectionist arguments threatened the profits of this global elite, the establishment used the ultimate political shortcut to neutralize him. They branded him with the "racist" label the immediate kiss of death designed to box a thinker into a corner so the public never listens to his platform. I do not care about the establishment's labels, nor do I care to alter my analysis to soothe partisan sensitivities. True intellectual honesty means stating plainly that Buchanan was entirely right not just about our hollowed out trade policy, but about his fundamental critique of artificial societal engineering.

Buchanan was right about the broken covenant made with the generation that bled to defeat tyranny in World War II . That massive sacrifice was an investment meant to secure a prosperous future for their descendants. If a grandfather had a secure, high wage job at a Ford plant, that tariff wall shielded his household long enough for his children to grow up, secure an education, and navigate a managed, gradual transition. 

When automation arrived, the worker’s child did not watch their community get hollowed out overnight by corporate outsourcing; instead, they could gradually transition into managing the very robotics and advanced systems that modernized the domestic plant.
This framework was fundamentally about preserving the sacred covenant forged by the generation that bled to defeat tyranny in World War II. That sacrifice was an investment meant to secure a prosperous future for their descendants. In a true, native born meritocracy, the grandson of that veteran should be the one stepping into high paying roles in the technology sector or advanced automation fields. Instead, the corporate political establishment utilized high-skill corporate pipelines, like the H-1B visa program, to entirely cut off the domestic pipeline. 

To maximize shareholder returns, corporate monopolies imported pre-trained foreign labor to suppress domestic wages, leaving the grandson of the veteran locked out of the modern economy. A sovereign nation must protect its high skill positions for its own citizens, ensuring that the fruits of national stability go to the lineage of the people who held the line to build it.

Part II: The Cyclical Paradox and the "Confederate Corner"

The real flaw that doomed Buchanan politically was not the establishment's weaponized labeling, but his own absolute, dogmatic inflexibility. He was an intellectual giant and a brilliant political architect, but he lacked the coalitional statecraft required to win executive office. By rigidly refusing to compromise on radioactive cultural tokens  at the time such as insisting that Mississippi preserve its historical flag exactly as it was he rendered his personal brand too heavy for a mass national coalition to carry. 

The irony is that conditions now perhaps could be right where things like that are superfluous and will not matter. They might actually be an advantage as more immigrants come  more relics of the America of yesterday year might come to bear as a benefit.  

 He was the ultimate coach who could draw the play perfectly on the chalkboard, but lacked the quarterback agility to run with the ball on the field. Buchanan fundamentally miscalculated the psychology of an electorate emerging from the prosperity of the 1980s. With the advent of NAFTA and globalized markets, the American public was presented with an immediate, intoxicating promise of corporate wealth and cheap consumer excess. 

When human beings get a taste of rapid material indulgence, their appetite for traditional values, household restraint, and multi generational discipline completely evaporates. Like a man who leaves a traditional marriage because a new partner offers an immediate, unhedged gratification he never experienced at home, the American public willingly walked away from its industrial foundation. They didn't care about the long-term betrayal of the domestic workforce because they were completely blindside-intoxicated by the short term transactional high of global capitalism.

This historical betrayal exposes a massive, cyclical realignment occurring within the grassroots American landscape a dynamic plainly visible within traditionalist right-wing spaces, what I informally call the online "Confederate corner." I do not use that term disparagingly at all; in fact, these digital enclaves are deeply fascinating because they actively preserve and highlight crucial elements of American heritage that are fundamentally good. Pundits operate under the lazy assumption that this modern traditionalist block will permanently align with standard pro corporate Republican economics. 

They completely miss the historical lesson of the pre 1960s Democratic Party. Historically, the Southern wing of the Democratic coalition combined intense, traditional social conservatism with a fiercely populistic, fiscally liberal economic agenda. They demanded massive infrastructure spending, public works, and agricultural subsidies because they viewed it as a natural right a material return for the wealth they felt the industrial North had systematically extracted from them.
That exact macro economic instinct is roaring back to the surface. The modern working class right has zero interest in country club fiscal austerity. 

They are transitioning into the new iteration of the old Southern Democrats: they remain fiercely traditional on social and cultural boundaries, but they expect the state to aggressively intervene to protect their industries, secure their housing stability, and manage their healthcare costs. They view this material security as a natural right owed to the descendants of the people who built the country.

I engage with these groups dispassionately. I am entirely aware that if certain individuals in that "Confederate corner" had their absolute choice, they might relegate a person of my background to a secondary condition. But in a free country, who cares? Every individual possesses the absolute right to an opinion, provided they maintain the baseline discipline of good manners. Because the institutional and constitutional boundaries of power are clear, they lack the capacity to enforce those prejudices. Therefore, we can bypass the tribal anxiety entirely, sit at the table like gentlemen, and engage in high level intellectual debate over the preservation of our shared heritage.

Part III: The FBA Alignment and the Recovery of Basics

If this upcoming populist reconstitution introduces a deliberate, strategic bridge to working class Black communities specifically framing it around the distinct lineage of Foundational Black Americans (FBAs) the resulting political alignment will be absolutely massive. A deep segment of the FBA population has naturally always held traditional, conservative values. For decades, they entered the Democratic coalition under the false assumption that they had to vote as an artificial monolith. But after enduring the radical cultural excesses of the modern left and the complete corporate abandonment of working-class interests, these communities are returning to basics.

For FBA families rooted straight down the line in a proud lineage of domestic military service, patriotism was never an option it was an ancestral duty. Their traditional value system rejects the progressive welfare apparatus. This isn't born out of a lack of empathy for those in need; it is an unyielding, multi generational recognition that state dependence, such as the public assistance pipeline, acts as an institutional weight on a family's head. It is a corporate shortcut designed to hook a community and suppress upward mobility.

When a family anchors its identity in hard work, generational pride, and military duty, the establishment’s attempt to scream "racist" to keep communities divided fails entirely. The moment the working class suits up, the underlying reality becomes obvious: their foundational principles are identical. They are all conservative, and they are good to go.

This cross demographic alignment finds its ultimate cultural expression in the unyielding authority of tradition. My mother was a  southerner she had breeding and good form . Her community stressed self reliance.She spoke  the universal language of unvarnished household discipline. She  had no patience for  focused pandering or corporate diversity double speak. 

She enforced  the absolute standard of accountability: “If you execute a necessary service, only God needs to know. If you perform an action simply to secure credit, your heart is in the wrong place do not bother with it entirely.” By replacing performative establishment lectures with this raw, maternal standard of quiet merit, a potential movement  can command immediate authority, uniting diverse communities under a shared, unyielding domestic compact.

Part IV: Geopolitical Totemism, Christian Zionism, and the Split Allegiance

The current party apparatus has traded rigorous, systemic stewardship for symbolic performance and top down demographic pandering. This institutional decay is most glaring in the establishment's dogmatic insistence on carrying foreign flags as mandatory domestic litmus tests.
This foreign hyper fixation caused a profound sense of alienation because elite consultants insisted on thrusting the geopolitical interests of an overseas homeland straight into the absolute center of local American elections. 

This overstep becomes particularly dangerous when driven by the mechanics of Christian Zionism. Within this framework, a massive proportion of the American political class conflates private biblical prophecy with statecraft, projecting a personal religious conviction directly onto the national stage.

True conservatism demands that a public official's first, absolute responsibility is to the United States Constitution and the internal stability of this country. When figures like Mike Huckabee and establishment politicians actively march inside an official U.S. Embassy to welcome a convicted thief like Jonathan Pollard who executed a catastrophic intelligence breach against the U.S. Navy the moral compass of our leadership is broken. Religion must remain a deeply personal experience; when an official puts it on blast on the government stage to underwrite a foreign asset, they are allowing their theological preference to outweigh their country duty.

Foreign leaders like Benjamin Netanyahu are not operating out of theological devotion; they are cold, calculating strategists who know how to play the American board. Netanyahu deliberately caters to this specific biblical demographic, utilizing focus focused trips to Israel and performative political theater to maintain an unbreakable domestic shield in Washington. The establishment covers this compromise by endlessly repeating that Israel is an unyielding ally. But true intellectual rigor requires a realistic threshold: An ally is an ally until it is not. When an international partner actively honors our spies, compromises our intelligence, and extracts our resources, an American leader must have the free-thinking independence to put the propaganda aside, evaluate the raw data, and ask: What are you going to do when that alliance no longer serves the survival of our country?

This miscalculation produced a profound "double whammy" for the establishment playbook. First, corporate consultants completely misread the younger Jewish electorate. For this newer generation, identity has largely decoupled from traditional or Zionist structures; their baseline identity is entirely secular and progressive. When forced to choose between modern liberal values and an intense foreign policy mandate, they refused to fall in line they walked away entirely.

 Second, by placing an outsized, unnatural pressure on the broader political movement to prioritize an external state, the establishment triggered a massive reactionary backlash. Instead of forcing compliance, this elite gatekeeping caused an elastic band to snap on the right. Prominent commentators like Tucker Carlson didn't just resist the pressure; they completely inverted it, retreating into an unyielding isolationism that explicitly rejects foreign capture and alienates the very establishment that attempted to enforce conformity.
When an independent analyst steps outside the approved script, the establishment instantly panics, using the media to smear them with unhinged labels like "foreign spy."

 Yet, this same political class remains completely silent when a sitting president operates a massive private golf course development and a luxury resort partnership in Qatar regularly interacting with foreign capital pipelines. When the elite class polices an independent commentator's speech while completely underwriting a politician's international business transactions, the gaslighting operation becomes glaringly obvious.

True conservatism holds a sacred reverence for institutional duty and sacrifice. The grand irony of the modern right is how easily a hyper polished media showman can convince the public that they are the ultimate archetype of patriotism, despite their own family possessing zero lineage of domestic military service. When a sitting president attempts to use their handpicked political board to force their own name onto the facade of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, or allows their administration to contemplate stripping the name of a legitimate World War World hero 2 Doris Miller, who earned the Navy Cross at Pearl Harbor off a multi billion dollar aircraft carrier to replace it with his own, the performance completely unravels. 

To families with deep military roots, this isn't patriotism. It is profound, unprecedented disrespect. It signals that a leader values personal branding and the magnification of their own ego over the quiet, multi-generational sacrifice of the heroes who held the line for this country.
The tragedy of the modern Republican Party is that its traditional stalwarts leaders like John Thune or Mitch McConnell failed to hold the line against either corporate outsourcing or performative populist excesses. 

Yet, select leaders understand the assignment. Senator Marco Rubio provides a precise blueprint for how an intelligent conservative navigates this landscape. Rubio didn’t "drink the Kool-Aid" of his own media hype. He isn't feeling himself to the point where he needs to constantly post on social media or manipulate news cycles for public adulation. In fact, Rubio possesses a natural shyness around the lens he does not actively crave or seek out the camera like these other performance artists. This quiet discipline is a profound asset. He executes his legislative and diplomatic directives with high-level intelligence without retreating into toxic online warfare. More importantly, on the trail, he presents himself and his wife as a complete, dignified package. That image of a stable family projects a steady hand and a baseline of decency that regular Americans are desperate for.

End of Volume I

text:
Your core distinction is the more useful one: immigration volume is not inherently the problem; the composition of who arrives, their skills, and the values and institutions they reinforce (or strain) is. Once the United States had continental scale, capital, and a relatively open institutional framework, selective immigration made more sense than undifferentiated volume, and that logic holds more strongly under modern globalization than it did in the 19th century.
Historically the country did scale population through immigration once it became a serious power. From the 1840s through the early 20th century, tens of millions arrived—predominantly from Europe—supplying labor for industry, railroads, and settlement of western land. Immigration accounted for a substantial share of population growth in several decades, and economic historians estimate that the 1880–1920 inflows raised later income per capita through a combination of skills, urban concentration, and innovation effects. The United States was not short of land or raw resources; it was short of people relative to the territory and productive opportunities available under its legal and technological conditions. Natural increase still dominated overall growth, but net migration was a large supplement.
Quality versus quantity was already a live concern among the founders and later policymakers. James Madison, in the 1790 naturalization debates, favored inducements for the “worthy part of mankind” precisely because the goal was not “merely to swell the catalogue of people” but to increase the wealth and strength of the community; those who acquired citizenship without adding to either were not desirable. Hamilton, George Washington, and others stressed the need for assimilation into common customs, measures, and laws so that newcomers (or their descendants) would become “one people.” Franklin worried about large unassimilated groups Germanizing Pennsylvania rather than being Anglicized. Later restrictions (literacy tests, national-origin quotas) reflected the same impulse once volumes rose and origin groups shifted. Modern economic research is consistent with the distinction: high-skilled inflows are more reliably associated with productivity, human-capital, and total-factor-productivity growth, while low-skilled inflows show weaker or more mixed effects on those metrics (though they can still expand labor supply and firm surplus in some models). Skill differences by origin were large even in the historical data—British and German immigrants, for example, patented at higher rates than some other European groups.
On values rather than color or mere numbers, the evidence supports treating selection and cultural compatibility as first-order. Assimilation occurs (earnings catch-up, English acquisition, name changes for children, intergenerational mobility), but the pace and completeness vary substantially by origin, education, legality of status, and whether the receiving environment expects it. Groups with higher average skills, stronger selection, or cultural proximity to existing norms tend to converge faster economically and civically. In a globalized talent market, high-skill migration is less about broad racial categories and more about individual human capital, English proficiency, and alignment with market and institutional norms; that is why policy focused on credentials, job offers, or points systems can operate with less emphasis on ancestry. At the same time, population-level patterns in educational attainment, fiscal contribution, crime, and political preferences by broad origin groups have not disappeared. Institutions (rule of law, property rights, selection mechanisms) matter more than ancestry per se, but they do not erase group differences in average outcomes overnight.
The practical implication is that the United States had (and still has) the land, capital, and infrastructure capacity to absorb large numbers, but the returns depend on who arrives and.

text:
Antonio Gramsci warned of the dangerous interval when the old order is dying and the new cannot yet be born. He called it the time of monsters.

I fear America has just entered one of those moments.

JD Vance is right. Trump's humiliating midterm defeat owes a great deal to the Iran war and the economic damage it has inflicted on ordinary Americans. But while Vance is examining why the Republicans lost, I'm rather more concerned about what Trump does next.

I've suspected for some time that Washington was deliberately holding back from another major escalation against Iran until the midterms were over. Another surge in oil prices, another hammering at the petrol pumps, and the Republicans would have faced an even angrier electorate.

Well, the votes are counted. The Republicans have been thrashed, and the political calculation that may have restrained Trump has changed.

And there's the danger.

Trump has already acknowledged that the war contributed to his defeat, yet insists he'd make the same decision again. That's hardly the language of a man contemplating the error of his ways.

My prediction is that he'll double down. With the Democrats not taking control of Congress until January, he has a window in which to escalate military operations, test the limits of his executive authority and attempt to impose his will before the new Congress can challenge him.

I hope I'm wrong. He could just as easily decide that another confrontation with Iran would deepen his political troubles. But Trump has never struck me as a man who responds particularly well to humiliation, especially when admitting defeat means admitting he was wrong.

And that brings me back to Gramsci and his monsters.

The American electorate has voted to restrain Trump, but the machinery of power remains in his hands. The ballot box has delivered its verdict, yet the new Congress cannot act on that verdict until January.

History teaches us that the most dangerous period isn't always when a leader is at the height of his power. Sometimes it's when that power begins slipping away, when wounded pride becomes political desperation and military force offers the illusion of restored authority.

Trump has lost the confidence of the electorate, but he hasn't lost command of the world's most powerful military.

And that is precisely why I believe the coming weeks could be more dangerous than anything we've witnessed so far.

The time of monsters may be upon us.

@PaulKnaggs, The Heartlands Tribune

🌒 MARKET STRUCTURE CENSUS — NOV. 4, 2026

Today, investors bought a future that hasn't arrived yet ... and punished some of the companies trying to build it.

The political result in Washington changed expectations about what could happen to data-centre expansion. Nothing has been stopped. No new restriction has taken effect. But markets don't always wait for a policy to become law before adjusting prices.

That was the tension running through the day.

The big companies positioned to benefit from AI gained. The chipmakers and data-centre builders fell. $AAPL  reached a record, while the wider technology trade was far less convincing.

At the same time, investors got the relief they'd been waiting for elsewhere. Oil dropped sharply, Treasury yields eased, and the Dow surged.

But notice what didn't happen: → the entire market didn't move together.

- The Dow rose 3.03%,
- while the Nasdaq-100 gained 0.91%. 
- Brent fell 8.7% to $94.62. 
- The 10-year yield finished at 4.89% after touching 4.96%.

And Bitcoin? It recovered $80,000, but the move came alongside $378 million in short liquidations in one hour. That's a lot of forced buying, not necessarily a fresh wave of committed investors.

The economic reports offered no single explanation either. ADP beat, ISM Services missed.

The market wasn't simply celebrating cheaper oil or lower rates. It was choosing which businesses might benefit from the next political and economic environment... and which might carry the cost.

→ Tomorrow's ETF flows will tell us more about Bitcoin. 

→ Friday's payrolls will matter for rate expectations. 

→ And next week's $25 billion Treasury auction will test whether buyers are comfortable lending money at these yields.

Today brought relief. It didn't settle the bill for tomorrow.

🔴 Trump Acknowledges Political Fallout: President Donald Trump has conceded that the war with Iran contributed significantly to Republicans' devastating midterm election losses, which handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress. According to The Washington Post and Reuters, Trump acknowledged that rising gasoline prices and public frustration with the conflict damaged Republican candidates nationwide.

⚠️ Trump Still Defends the War: Despite recognizing the political consequences, Trump insists that launching the military campaign was the right decision. Speaking to The Wall Street Journal, he declared, "I did the right thing. I would have done it again." His remarks suggest that electoral losses have not fundamentally changed his defense of the intervention.

🇺🇸 JD Vance Pushes for an End to the Conflict: Vice President JD Vance has taken a stronger position, directly blaming the Iran war for Republican defeats. According to Reuters, Vance argued that the administration should prioritize ending the conflict, addressing inflation and restoring its focus on domestic economic concerns.

💣 Military Escalation Remains Under Consideration: Reuters reports that administration officials are still considering renewed major combat operations against Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly favor additional military pressure, believing Iran cannot be trusted to honor a negotiated agreement.

🕊️ Diplomatic Negotiations Offer Another Path: According to Axios, Vance and White House envoy Steve Witkoff support pursuing an agreement with Tehran. Qatar and Pakistan have been involved in mediation efforts, while Iranian officials have indicated a willingness to continue negotiations under certain conditions.

💰 Economic Consequences Could Be Significant: Renewed American strikes could trigger Iranian retaliation, disrupt oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and push gasoline prices higher. The Council on Foreign Relations warns that another escalation could deepen the economic consequences of a conflict that has already become a major domestic political issue.

🏛️ Democratic Control Changes the Political Equation: With Democrats taking control of Congress, Trump faces increased scrutiny over military operations, war spending and his administration's handling of the conflict. Congressional investigations and challenges to additional military action could complicate his decisions.

🔥 Trump Faces Three Major Choices: The president can pursue a negotiated settlement, authorize another military offensive or maintain economic pressure while postponing further attacks. Axios reports that competing factions within his administration favor different approaches. Trump has indicated that he is in no rush to make a final decision, leaving the future of the Iran conflict uncertain.

HYPERGROWTH #8 SANDISK $SNDK IS 56% OFF ITS HIGH:

Sandisk (SNDK) at $1,037.40, -$89.12 / -7.91% on Wednesday.

Sandisk is #8 on the Hypergrowth Len5 with sales nearly five times a year earlier, and a 26% fall in five sessions has not touched the reason it is there. The Milpitas, California company makes NAND flash, the memory chips in phones, laptops and the drives inside AI data centers, and it earned $8.1 billion in the September quarter as those data centers bought every chip on offer. Wednesday's fall came with the memory group on the election, after a cautious forecast from the Japanese partner that makes its chips and two analyst cuts, and the slope of the December-quarter forecast is what could move it off the Len5.

Hypergrowth wants sales multiplying at a young business, and Sandisk, on its own since Western Digital spun it off in February 2025, sold $11.0 billion of memory in the September quarter against $2.3 billion a year earlier. What would knock it off the Hypergrowth Len5: a quarter in which revenue falls from the one before, which a turn in NAND prices would bring; the forecast is +12% at the midpoint after +23% in September and +51% in June, and sales to consumers already fell 29% from the June quarter. It fits the Quality Len5 on its own books, $9.4 billion left after making the chips, an $8.1 billion profit and no debt, and it is not on the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations or Income Len5es: 56% under the June 22 high of $2,354.39, a profit that was $112 million a year ago is not yet durable, and no dividend.

The September quarter, reported October 29:
- Revenue $11.0B, +378% from a year ago and +23% from June; data center $4.8B, +61% from June; consumer products $397M, -29% from June; adjusted profit $49.51 a share against its own $44 to $46 forecast.
- December-quarter forecast: revenue $12.2B to $12.6B; adjusted profit $55 to $57 a share, or $6.88 to $7.13 after the 8-for-1 split that takes effect November 20.

Rich Smith of The Motley Fool put Wednesday's fall on the election and the AI regulation a Democratic Congress may bring; David Moadel of 24/7 Wall St added Kioxia Holdings (285A in Tokyo), which makes Sandisk's chips with it and forecast NAND prices roughly flat this quarter after a mid-20% rise last quarter. Fox Advisors cut Sandisk to Equal Weight on Monday and Wells Fargo cut its price target to $1,300 on October 30; the shares are down 26% from the October 28 close and still up about 350% this year.

The December quarter, due around January 28, a date Sandisk has not confirmed, is the one that can move the Len5 seat: revenue against the $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion forecast says whether the slope is flattening or turning, and consumer sales against $397 million say whether buyers are balking at the price.

DEEP-VALUE PICK DOLLAR GENERAL $DG, SUED, UP 8.5%:

Dollar General (DG) at $141.64, +$11.12 / +8.52% on Wednesday.

Dollar General is a Deep-Value and Special-Situations pick for a profit still climbing back from its 2024 low, and Wednesday's $2.4 billion gain on a vote in Washington moved the price closer to where that Len5 lets go. The Goodlettsville, Tennessee chain of 21,148 small stores announced nothing; dollar stores led the market on hopes that a Democratic Congress restores the food aid its shoppers lost this year. The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states sued it nine days ago over checkout prices, and that bill is the open number.

Deep-Value and Special-Situations wants a sound business priced under a cautious value of what it earns, and Dollar General's earning power is the half that fits: profit fell from $2.4 billion in fiscal 2022 to $1.1 billion two years later, recovered to $1.5 billion last year, and the company forecasts about $1.7 billion for this year. The price half is thinner than it was: about 18 times that forecast after a 49% rise from the November 2025 low of $95.11, 10% under the February 26 high of $158.23. What would knock it off the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5: the shares at that February high with the forecast unchanged, or customer traffic turning negative after five straight quarters of growth. It fits the Quality Len5, profitable with obligations at half of owners' equity, and it is not on the Momentum, Quality-Value, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es; a profit that halved in two years is not yet the durable one Quality-Value wants.

The July quarter, reported August 27:
- Sales $11.3B, +5.2%; same-store sales +3.5% on 2.0% more customers; profit $2.48 a share against $1.86; the year raised to $7.80 to $8.00 a share.
Donny Lau, Dollar General's chief financial officer, said in June that SNAP dollars distributed this year fell significantly; the Associated Press put Wednesday's dollar-store rally on hopes that Democrats reverse some of last year's cuts to federal food assistance.

On October 26 the FTC and 20 states sued Dollar General in federal court in Nashville, alleging that for years its registers charged more than its shelf tags and ads, behind nearly 30,000 customer complaints since 2019; Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said the company "has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers." Dollar General will "defend this litigation vigorously" and called the demand "orders of magnitude larger than" any realistic assessment; the shares fell 3.2% that day.

Dollar General reports the October quarter around December 3, a date it has not confirmed; analysts expect about $1.40 a share, and customer traffic against the summer's 2.0% is the quarter's number. The FTC's number, the one neither side has put in public, comes on the court's clock, not the company's.

Sysco (SYY) at $76.94, +$2.83 / +3.82% on Wednesday.

Sysco is a Quality-Value pick, and Tuesday's 9% fall on a quarter that met its own profit forecast widened the discount that Len5 needs. The Houston company, the largest U.S. distributor of food to restaurants, hospitals and schools, earned what analysts expected and sold less than they expected, because food prices barely rose. The $29 billion purchase of Restaurant Depot closes early next year on $21 billion of new debt, and that debt is what could move Sysco off the Len5.

Quality-Value wants a durable business at a price its own profit justifies. Sysco has the durable half: its sales to independent restaurants grew 2.7% by case count in a quarter when restaurant traffic across the industry fell 2%, by Black Box Intelligence's count. The price half arrived on Tuesday: 16% under the February 17 high of $91.85, about 15 times the profit Sysco forecasts for this fiscal year. What would knock it off the Quality-Value Len5: the Restaurant Depot debt, about 4.5 times a year's EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax and depreciation) at closing, still there after the two years Sysco gave itself to cut it; or the shares back near $92 with the forecast unchanged. It fails the Quality Len5 on its books, $13.8 billion of debt against $4.0 billion of owners' equity, and it is on none of the Momentum, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es.

The September quarter, reported Tuesday before the open:
- Sales $21.7B, +2.8%, against $22.0B expected; adjusted profit $1.19 a share, +3.5%, as expected; product cost inflation 0.3% against the 1.4% Sysco planned on.
Flat food prices mean flat sales for Sysco even when the cases keep moving. Sysco now expects sales growth at the low end of its 6% to 7% range and holds adjusted profit growth at 9% to 11%; the shares fell 9.3% on Tuesday. Restaurant Depot, the warehouse chain where small restaurants shop for themselves, costs about $29.1 billion including debt in a deal signed March 30 and due to close between late December and late March.

Wednesday's bounce came with US Foods Holding (USFD) at $109.93, +$8.57 / +8.46% on Wednesday, a 52-week high the day before its own report; US Foods, on none of the Len5es we weigh at 31 times the past year's profit, reports Thursday before the open and says whether 0.3% inflation is Sysco's problem or the industry's. Sysco's own December quarter lands around January 26, a date it has not confirmed; case volume against the 2.5% it promised for the year is the first figure on the page, and 9% to 11% profit growth on flat prices is the durable half holding while the debt arrives.

text:
𝐇𝐲𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐍𝐞𝐰𝐬 – 𝐍𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟎𝟒, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔

Bitcoin’s sharp rebound followed an election-driven selloff, but the recovery is testing whether leveraged relief buying can overcome weak fund flows and persistent security concerns.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰

Bitcoin climbed back above $80,000 on November 4 after sliding toward $75,600 around the U.S. midterm results, as wider markets recovered and traders betting against crypto were forced to close positions. That reversal lifted major assets, but it does not yet establish that spot demand has returned: U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded about $1.16 billion in net outflows over three sessions, while short liquidations accounted for much of the day’s market-wide forced closures. The political result adds another uncertainty rather than an immediate rule change. Democrats’ control of both chambers could complicate the stalled CLARITY Act, even as SEC and CFTC initiatives under existing authority continue.

The market’s other defining thread was the cost of operational risk. Binance said it had replenished 98% of assets affected by the October 29 theft and would cover the remaining loss, but funds linked to the attackers continued moving through cross-chain routes after THORChain resumed swaps. Separate reported breaches at Mercado Bitcoin and BitMart broadened concern beyond one exchange, while investigators’ allegation of a major theft involving Crédit Mutuel Arkéa remains unconfirmed by the bank.

At the same time, regulated tokenization is advancing through institutional infrastructure rather than an overnight move to always-on stock trading. Morgan Stanley began using DTCC’s tokenization service, while the NYSE’s proposed venue remains under development and subject to approval. Together, these developments show a market recovering in price while still demanding evidence: sustainable inflows, dependable security and rules that survive political change.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐧𝐚𝐩𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐭

• $BTC: $80,443, +4.0%
• ETH: $2,423, +6.6%
• BNB: $719.42, +3.2%
• XRP: $1.30, +2.2%
• SOL: $95.51, +2.9%
• ZEC: $1,346.65, +10.59%
• U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded about $1.16 billion in net outflows across three sessions from October 30 to November 3.
• Crypto liquidations totaled about $913.83 million over 24 hours, with short positions accounting for $554.27 million and long positions for $359.55 million.
• The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75%–4% on October 28; its statement said inflation remained elevated.
𝐓𝐨𝐩 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬

𝟏. 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐫𝐞𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐯𝐞 $𝟖𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐚𝐬 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞

Bitcoin recovered from a seven-week low near $75,600 to trade above $80,000 on November 4, reversing much of the election-linked decline. The move came as broader markets recovered and short positions were squeezed: crypto liquidations reached about $913.83 million over 24 hours, including $554.27 million in short liquidations. The scale of forced closures helps explain the speed of the bounce, but it is not evidence by itself of new spot buying. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had lost about $1.16 billion over three sessions, while analysts identified $84,000–$85,500 as a potential resistance zone. A durable recovery therefore still needs demand that persists after leveraged positions have been cleared.

𝟐. 𝐁𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐢𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 $𝟔.𝟑 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐟𝐭

Binance said it had replenished 98% of the assets affected by its October 29 security breach and would use company funds to cover the remainder, with limited liquidity potentially delaying purchases of the remaining tokens. The exchange said attackers compromised engineers through tampered software and a fake job interview, then used stolen credentials to move 233.46 million XRP from five hot wallets in four minutes before stealing other cryptocurrencies. Binance reported freezing or intercepting about $2.85 billion and rebuilding affected wallet systems; the FBI attributed the attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, an allegation Pyongyang denies. On-chain investigations indicate that laundering activity continued through new wallets and cross-chain services, and THORChain’s restored swaps reopened one route used to convert stolen funds. The incident has made access controls and transaction approvals–not just whether assets are held offline–central questions for exchanges and their customers.

𝟑. 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐚𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐥𝐞𝐲 𝐣𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐃𝐓𝐂𝐂’𝐬 𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐨𝐤𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞

Morgan Stanley has begun tokenizing U.S. stocks and Treasury securities through DTCC’s blockchain-based service, which represents securities held in DTC custody while preserving their existing ownership rights and investor protections. The service supports Canton Network and DTCC’s private Besu network, with more integrations planned for 2027; Morgan Stanley is among 20 participating institutions. This regulated model is distinct from a synthetic token that merely tracks a stock’s price, because the tokens are tied to securities held in custody. Morgan Stanley’s separate plan to offer tokenized equities through its alternative trading system is expected in the first quarter of 2027, while the NYSE’s proposed tokenized venue remains in development and requires regulatory approval. The near-term shift is institutional preparation, not evidence that round-the-clock blockchain trading has already replaced traditional market infrastructure.

𝟒. 𝐌𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐚𝐝𝐨 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐡𝐨𝐭-𝐰𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐭 𝐛𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡

Mercado Bitcoin said it would begin restoring account access in stages, initially allowing customers to view balances while keeping trading, withdrawals and transfers suspended pending independent security checks. The exchange said it would use company funds to replace affected assets and had helped freeze more than $15 million, while blockchain analysts estimated losses exceeding $46 million. Chainalysis separately described the incident as approximately $49 million and said nearly $10 million had been frozen with partners’ assistance, stressing that a freeze is not the same as recovered funds or customer reimbursement. BitMart confirmed a November 2 breach and said its preliminary investigation suggested the same attackers may have targeted Mercado Bitcoin; researchers traced about $391,000 from BitMart-linked wallets to addresses associated with the Mercado Bitcoin exploit. The two incidents add to pressure on exchanges to explain their losses, customer access arrangements and security changes clearly, rather than treating asset tracing as proof of recovery.

𝟓. 𝐒𝐄𝐂 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐟𝐟 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐥𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

The SEC’s Division of Corporation Finance said it would not recommend enforcement over Canton Coin’s programmatic issuance without securities registration, provided the network operates under the conditions presented. Staff described the token as a digital commodity based on its role in Canton Network operations and the network’s lack of a central controlling party, but the position is limited to the specified issuance arrangements. It is staff guidance, not a binding Commission rule or a blanket approval of the token or other transactions involving it. The statement arrives as financial institutions expand tokenization activity on Canton, including through DTCC’s service, giving participants a more concrete reference point for one issuance model. The broader legal status of other assets and transactions still depends on their facts and applicable law.

𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 & 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐲

The election reshaped the political context for U.S. crypto rules, but it did not itself change existing law. Democrats’ control of both chambers could make negotiations over the stalled CLARITY Act harder, particularly as lawmakers debate investor protections, anti-money-laundering safeguards and ethics restrictions. Industry leaders have argued that durable rules will need bipartisan support; meanwhile, the SEC and CFTC are pursuing work under existing authority, including proposals and guidance that have not all been finalized. The SEC staff’s conditional position on Canton Coin adds specificity to how one programmatic issuance may be assessed, without establishing a general classification rule. Outside the U.S., Hong Kong passed legislation requiring covered crypto service providers to collect customer tax-residency and transaction information from 2027, with exchanges of data with eligible partner jurisdictions planned for 2028. These developments point to a regulatory landscape being built through agency action and jurisdiction-specific reporting even as U.S. legislation remains uncertain.

𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 & 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤

The Binance theft remained the clearest warning that a large exchange’s security depends on the full chain of access, signing and approval controls. Binance’s account describes a months-long campaign involving tampered software, fraudulent recruitment and compromised credentials; it says affected customer assets have been almost entirely replenished, while investigators continue to trace stolen funds. Separately, Mercado Bitcoin and BitMart disclosed breaches, and the bank theft alleged by ZachXBT remains unconfirmed by Crédit Mutuel Arkéa. Holders should treat unsolicited support messages and recovery offers with particular caution: reports warn that scammers impersonate police or wallet support to obtain recovery phrases, while many advertised recovery-service claims are unverified. Use official channels, never disclose a recovery phrase, and treat a freeze or a promise of recovery as distinct from funds being returned.

𝐀𝐥𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐬 & 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐬

Zcash drew attention ahead of its NU7 upgrade, scheduled around November 5. The upgrade targets 25-second block intervals and directs 60% of transaction fees to a reserve for future mining rewards without changing the maximum supply; node operators need compatible software, and holders with funds in the original Sprout pool must move them to supported addresses before activation. Separately, Zcash Community Grants withdrew a proposal to redirect about 98,000 ZEC toward mining rewards after community criticism, leaving other funding proposals unresolved. NEAR’s governance body approved a gradual reduction in the annual token issuance ceiling from 2.5% to 1.6% over two years, but the change still requires further review and implementation; lower issuance may also reduce staking yields. Stellar’s Bell upgrade is live on testnet, with validators scheduled to vote on mainnet activation on November 23; it adds tools for managing multiple customer balances and lets smart contracts verify post-quantum signatures, but does not change network-level transaction signatures. These changes show protocols balancing supply, governance and infrastructure upgrades, while near-term token prices remain exposed to broader market conditions.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐖𝐚𝐭𝐜𝐡

• November 5: Zcash’s NU7 activation is expected around this date; node operators need compatible software, and affected Sprout-pool holders must move funds to supported addresses before activation.
• November 6 and 10: Further court filings are due in the case challenging the CFTC’s approval of single-stock perpetual futures; the products remain available while the court considers a preliminary injunction.
• November 6: The October U.S. employment report is scheduled for release and could affect interest-rate expectations and risk appetite.
• November 16: Trap Map’s pre-lawsuit notice to Bubblemaps sets a response deadline; no court filing or finding of misconduct has been established.
• November 17–19: Pi’s first Ecosystem Summit is scheduled, though it is not a guaranteed price catalyst.
• November 23: Stellar validators are scheduled to vote on Bell’s mainnet activation.
• December 10: A hearing is scheduled on Justin Sun’s request for sanctions against World Liberty Financial and its lawyers.
• January 2027: The Ethereum Foundation is due to review its post-quantum roadmap; the review could clarify how developer targets relate to the existing deadline.
• January 2027: The next U.S. Congress is scheduled to begin, when the change in committee control may shape crypto legislation and oversight.
• February 2027: Congressional investigations into Trump-linked crypto businesses could begin as early as this month.
• End of February 2027: Existing U.K. crypto firms must submit complete authorization applications to qualify for temporary operating status under the FCA’s finalized stablecoin rules.
• First quarter of 2027: Morgan Stanley expects to launch its separate tokenized-equity trading service through its alternative trading system.
• 2027: Hong Kong’s crypto-asset reporting requirements are due to begin for covered businesses; the jurisdiction plans to start exchanging relevant data with eligible partners in 2028.

From the bottom of my heart, THANK YOU!

To everyone who supported me, voted for me, volunteered, donated, knocked on doors, made phone calls, put up signs, or simply offered a word of encouragement throughout this campaign — I cannot thank you enough.

Running for Congress has been an incredible journey. I’ve had the privilege of meeting so many wonderful people across Illinois’ 11th Congressional District, listening to your concerns, hearing your stories, and sharing my vision for a better future.

I am especially grateful to my family, friends, and the dedicated volunteers who gave so much of their time and energy. Your faith in me, your hard work, and your friendship mean more than you will ever know.

While elections come and go, the relationships we’ve built and the friendships we’ve made will last far beyond this campaign.

I’ve spent much of my life serving others — in the United States Navy, in my professional career, and as Mayor of Elburn. That commitment to public service doesn’t end with an election.

To everyone who cast a vote for me, thank you for placing your trust and confidence in me. It has truly been an honor.

God bless you, God bless Illinois, and God bless the United States of America! 🇺🇸

Jeff Walter

text:
INCOME #6 LCI $LCII IS WORTH MORE THAN THE CASH BID:

LCI Industries (LCII) at $104.28, +$2.43 / +2.39% on Wednesday.

LCI Industries is #6 on the Income Len5, and the dividend that earns it the seat has an expiry date: the all-stock merger with Patrick Industries that shareholders vote on November 18. The Elkhart, Indiana company makes the axles, chassis and windows that go into recreational vehicles, and it kept paying $1.15 a quarter through a year in which RV makers cut their build by about a sixth. A private-equity firm offered $101 a share in cash last week; the board said no, and Patrick's rally since has made its stock worth more than the cash anyway. The quarter arrives Thursday morning.

Income wants cash paid to owners that the business covers with room to spare, and LCI's dividend takes about half of its forecast profit: $1.15 a quarter, about 4.4% a year at Wednesday's close, against $8.25 to $8.75 a share of adjusted profit forecast for 2026, and $346 million of operating cash flow in the year to June covered $112 million of dividends three times. What would knock it off the Income Len5: the Patrick merger closing, expected in the first half of 2027. Each LCI share becomes 1.2440 Patrick shares, and at the $0.47 a quarter Patrick pays now those carry about $2.34 a year, half of LCI's $4.60, unless the combined board lifts the payout. It fits the Quality Len5 on its own books, profitable with $852.6 million of debt under $1.43 billion of owners' equity, and it is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations or Hypergrowth Len5es, because its price now follows Patrick's stock rather than its own profit.

The two offers:
- Patrick Industries (PATK) at $84.68, +$3.28 / +4.03% on Wednesday: 1.2440 of its shares for each LCI share, worth $84.64 an LCI share when the proxy was priced on October 16 and $105.34 at Wednesday's close.
- Monomoy Capital Partners: $101 a share in cash, non-binding, disclosed October 28; the board rejected it on October 30, saying LCI's own plan "implies a midpoint discounted cash flow value in excess of $150 per share," its estimate of what the business's future cash is worth today.
Patrick has risen 24% since October 16, so a cash bid worth $11 more than the stock deal when it arrived is now worth $4 less, and LCI closed Wednesday 1% under the value of 1.244 Patrick shares. Patrick, which makes the same RV parts, is on none of the Len5es we weigh, at 21 times the past year's profit with a 2.2% yield.

LCI reports the September quarter Thursday before the open, with the call at 8:30am ET; analysts expect about $2.04 a share against $1.97 a year ago, on sales near $995 million against $1.04 billion. The dividend declared with it, $1.15 or not, is the Income number; the vote two weeks later, and Patrick's price on that day, decide how long LCI keeps paying it.

Not investment advice.

text:
As a political example, let’s take Sherrod Brown’s market odds of winning Ohio compared to the price offered on Democratic Senate control with 52+ seats.

Obviously they’re correlated to a substantial degree. It’s unlikely for the Dems to win that large of a Senate majority while losing Ohio. Plus it’s more likely for them to also lose Michigan in this instance.

But the key question is how much is this correlation reflected in the market price on Senate seats?

For instance, in the extreme sense, if the correlation between Brown & D52+ was actually 1.00, both markets *should* have the same price. It’s effectively the same bet. 

So if one is 1-2 cents off, there’s literally an immediate “edge” (in a similar way line shopping between -122 and -117 is on sportsbooks). And if it’s off by way larger, there may be a profitable arbitrage opportunity to take what are effectively the same positions on both sides.

Simply finding the best price isn’t an edge in and of itself, but in political markets this cycle you could have analyzed correlative factors and scoured the board where certain markets were upwards of 20 cents off in relation.

$CBRS (Cerebras) fell 6.10% today, closing at $91.85 and hitting a NEW ALL-TIME LOW of $90.28 intraday.

Meanwhile, the Dow surged 3.03%, its best day in approximately 18 months. The S&P 500 gained 1.58%, and the Nasdaq rose 1.44%.

@Cerebras is now trading roughly 50% BELOW its $185 IPO price.

But I think the market may be overlooking something important.

What if the very thing causing today's AI infrastructure selloff could actually create TWO major tailwinds for Cerebras?

The selloff across neocloud and AI infrastructure stocks comes amid growing fears that the Democrats' midterm victories could lead to tougher restrictions on new data center construction.

Texas is at the center of those concerns.

Democrat Gina Hinojosa just won the Texas governor's race after campaigning on a moratorium on new data center approvals.

That's particularly concerning for companies with billions invested in Texas facilities that haven't been completed.

But here's where Cerebras is different.

Cerebras already has an operational data center in Dallas, and its publicly disclosed near term expansion includes:

• Alabama: 40 MW of planned capacity, with the first 15 MW targeted for December 2026 and the remainder in Q1 2027.

• Minnesota: Another 40 MW project already under development, with initial revenue expected in Q1 2027.

• Other locations: Additional capacity secured across the U.S., Canada, and Europe.

Based on disclosed projects, I haven't identified another new Texas facility that Cerebras's near term growth depends on.

So while other companies may face significant delays bringing new Texas capacity online, Cerebras appears to have more geographically diversified expansion plans.

TAILWIND #1: Existing operational data center capacity becomes more valuable.

If AI compute demand keeps accelerating while new supply becomes more difficult to bring online, existing capacity could command an even larger premium.

Companies with functioning infrastructure and advanced-stage projects could find themselves in an increasingly advantageous position.

But TAILWIND #2 is what I find even more interesting.

If building new data centers becomes harder, companies aren't going to simply abandon their AI ambitions.

They're going to look for ways to squeeze MORE COMPUTE out of the infrastructure they've already built.

And that's where Cerebras's disaggregated inference technology could become incredibly valuable.

Rather than relying entirely on GPUs for AI inference, operators can potentially combine GPU infrastructure with Cerebras systems.

GPUs handle prefill, while Cerebras handles decode, generating tokens at extremely high speeds.

By combining these architectures, companies could dramatically improve throughput and efficiency without needing an entirely new data center.

Cerebras's partnerships with AMD and AWS already target improvements of up to 5x in specific measures of inference efficiency and capacity.

Think about that.

In a world where data center space and power become increasingly constrained, technologies capable of generating substantially more AI output from a given footprint could become dramatically more valuable.

Adding Cerebras still requires hardware, power, and integration, but it could offer an attractive alternative to simply building more traditional GPU capacity.

And Cerebras doesn't necessarily need customers to replace their existing GPUs. Its technology could actually make those GPU investments more productive.

This is what I think the market is missing.

Cerebras isn't just another AI infrastructure company dependent on building more data centers.

It's also developing technology that could help the entire industry maximize the infrastructure it already has.

Of course, Cerebras isn't immune to permitting, construction, or execution risks. But not every AI infrastructure company has the same exposure.

My takeaway: The market is selling AI infrastructure stocks because it may become harder to build new data centers.

But what if those same restrictions ultimately accelerate demand for the very technology Cerebras is developing?

At $91.85, with $CBRS hitting all-time lows while the broader market rallies, I think that's a possibility worth paying attention to.

My long-term thesis on Cerebras remains unchanged. I remain LONG the stock and continue to add shares.

FOR 17 MONTHS, A TEENAGE GIRL WAS MISSING. NOW WE KNOW WHAT SHE ENDURED BEHIND CLOSED DOORS.

She was held captive in an Oregon home, repeatedly assaulted, cut off from the outside world, and forced to remove her own braces with PLIERS so she would be harder to identify.

She was just 15 years old when she disappeared.

Kylie Arellano vanished from her home in Garden City, Utah, on May 29, 2025. For nearly a year and a half, her family and investigators searched for answers.

Now 17, Kylie has been found alive.

Federal investigators allege that Adam Hunter Harmel (39) met Kylie online, offered her money to travel to Oregon, and drove to Utah to pick her up.

Once in Oregon, Harmel allegedly threw her phone into a river, prevented her from leaving, and subjected her to repeated physical and sexual assaults.

But after 17 months, Kylie found a way to reach someone.

She reportedly contacted another child through an online gaming platform. That child told a parent, who contacted the FBI. Agents eventually listened in on a video call as Kylie described what had happened to her.

On November 1, 2026, authorities rescued Kylie from a home in Huntington, Oregon.

Harmel was arrested and is now facing federal charges.

Think about that. A teenager held captive for 17 months managed to find a way to get help through an online game.

And because another child spoke up, and a parent took it seriously, Kylie is finally free.

We know how investigators say she ended up in Oregon. What is difficult to comprehend is how she could be held there for 17 months without anyone discovering what was happening.

But today, the most important thing is that Kylie survived.

text:
I'm Japanese.

I live in Tokyo. I have never been to America.

For the past month, I've been writing stories here about Americans. Some of you laughed. A lot of you cried. Some of you asked me if they were true.

Honest answer: they're inspired by real moments. I change names and details.

But this post is different.

Every word of this one is true.

Because this one is about you.

Thousands of you replied to those stories. I read them late at night in my apartment in Tokyo, one by one. And somewhere along the way, I realized something.

You were telling me better stories than I was telling you.

Here are some of the things Americans told a stranger in Japan this month.

A pilot told me he once helped shut down an entire airport so a mother duck and her six babies could cross the runway. He coordinated with air traffic control. For ducks. He told me like it was a normal Tuesday.

A father told me he has four daughters, and one of them is walking around with his left kidney. That was the whole reply. Eleven words. Like a fun fact.

A woman told me she was rescued from a hurricane by strangers in their own boats. Nobody called them. They just came. All she wrote was: "God bless people with boats."

A soldier told me he once sat down for lunch at the Dallas airport in uniform. One stranger bought his table a round. Another bought their lunch. A third bought another round. He never found out who any of them were.

A man from Brazil told me he was once filming a video about how kind Americans are. In the middle of filming, a stranger walked up and offered him a beer.

A woman told me that Dolly Parton's father couldn't read. So Dolly grew up and started sending free books to children.

A woman corrected me. I had written that American dads can't braid hair. She told me her father braided hers every single morning, all through elementary school.

She was right. I have never been so happy to be wrong.

A man told me that at the Boston Marathon, the crowds thin out near the end, but somebody always stays until the very last runner goes by.

A woman told me her mother had Alzheimer's. For years, her father told her mother the story of their life together, over and over, so she wouldn't lose it.

And a woman told me that just today, she was too tired to lift something into the trunk of her car. A young couple walked by. She asked. The young man helped.

Just today.

You also made me laugh until I couldn't breathe.

I asked for the most American sentence in five words. You gave me "Hold my beer. Watch this." You gave me "That's not enough ranch." One woman broke the rules and wrote, "How about three? God Bless America." Nobody complained. Not one American said, "That's only three."

One woman reports her tissue count on every story. "OK, that's three tissues so far today." Then, on the next one: "Four. Dang."

One man told me, "I'm never deleting this app."

One woman said Japanese people are a blessing, and she will personally "have words" with anyone who says otherwise. I have never felt so safe in my life.

One of you called me "Sensei." I'm not a teacher. You are.

And one woman told me that she has actually said, out loud, in real life:

"There's a bald eagle sitting on my truck."

Here's what I noticed.

Almost none of you told me about yourselves.

You told me about your father. A stranger with a boat. A pilot. The people who stayed for the last runner. The young man at the trunk.

And the few of you who did the good thing yourselves? You told it like it was nothing. You gave away a kidney and described it in eleven words.

You are a country that remembers every kind thing anyone ever did for you, and forgets every kind thing you ever did yourself.

So I'll remember them for you.

A lot of you wrote some version of the same sentence.

"I needed this."

"It's hard to be an American right now."

"I don't know if we're still good."

One woman wrote to me late at night. She couldn't sleep. She had been reading all the awful news. She said she might be a little discouraged, but she will never stop being an American who loves her country.

Another woman told me she cries after every story. She thinks it's because she's carrying old grief. Then she wrote, "I guess that means I'm alive."

I read that one at 3 a.m. in Tokyo. And I cried too.

I started writing these stories to cheer you up.

I never expected you to cheer me up.

So, thank you.

To the pilot who stopped an airport. To the dad with one kidney. To the people with boats. To the strangers at the Dallas airport. To the dad who braided hair before work. To the ones who stay for the last runner. To the husband who kept telling the story. To the young man at the trunk. To the woman counting tissues. To the woman who can't sleep and still loves her country.

To the bald eagle on the truck.

Thank you.

And to everyone who asked me if Americans are still good:

I'm Japanese. I've never been to America. I'm not the right person to answer that.

But I know who is.

Scroll down.

That's America.
